lead: This unit is about the electronics that shift, steer, brake and protect a moving car. After it you can explain how a transmission control unit picks a gear, how cruise and adaptive cruise hold a gap, how ABS and ESP control wheel slip and yaw, and how a PI controller is tuned for a speed loop. You can also describe active suspension, airbags and the ADAS layers that sit above them.
about: Unit 5 covers the electronic systems that decide how a vehicle moves and how it protects the people inside. Chapter 5.1 starts at the gearbox, where a transmission control unit picks shift points. Chapter 5.2 adds speed control, and 5.3 makes steering assist depend on speed. Chapter 5.4 explains anti-lock braking and traction control, the wheel-slip systems that 5.5, the electronic stability program, builds on. Chapter 5.6 looks at active suspension for ride control. Chapter 5.7 turns to passive safety and airbags, and 5.8 groups the warning and assist functions under ADAS. Chapter 5.9 closes with the PI and PD controllers that sit inside cruise control and every other speed loop.

chapters.idea: A transmission control unit reads throttle and speed, picks a shift point from a shift map, and then controls clutch pressure so the shift is quick and smooth.
chapters.depth: Shift map (throttle against vehicle speed) and the shift schedule; torque converter and lock-up clutch; hydraulic circuit with solenoid valves and line pressure; shift quality by engine torque reduction and adaptive learning of clutch fill. The four common layouts: AMT (automated manual), DCT (dual-clutch), CVT with belt and pulleys, and the conventional automatic. Some syllabi call the unit the TCU (transmission control unit) or the gearbox ECU. Keep gear-tooth and planetary gearset mechanics out.

figure.title: Electronic transmission control loop
figure.aria: A loop where inputs reach the TCU shift map, which drives solenoid valves and clutch packs to select a gear ratio, with output shaft speed fed back.

chapters.example: A car runs at 60 km/h in top gear. Wheel radius r = 0.30 m, final drive ratio 3.50, top gear ratio 0.70. Wheel angular speed gives wheel rpm = v/(2πr) × 60 = (16.67 m/s ÷ 1.885 m) × 60 = 531 rpm. Engine speed = 531 × 3.50 × 0.70 = 1300 rpm. If the TCU downshifts to a direct gear of 1.00, engine speed = 531 × 3.50 × 1.00 = 1857 rpm. The downshift raises engine speed by 557 rpm, which is the torque rise the driver feels.
chapters.trap: Leaving out the final drive when converting wheel speed to engine speed, and assuming shifts happen at a fixed vehicle speed — the shift map also reads throttle, so a light throttle upshifts early.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 for throttle, engine torque and power; Unit 3 for speed and position sensors.
chapters.leave: Planetary gearset kinematics and clutch plate design; the CAN frames that carry these signals go to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Cruise control holds a set speed with a closed loop on throttle, and adaptive cruise control adds a gap loop that can also apply the brakes.
chapters.depth: Set, resume, cancel and coast functions; speed error → PI controller → throttle; why the integral term is needed on a hill; adaptive cruise: forward sensor (77 GHz radar or camera), time gap measured in seconds, target selection, cut-in handling, stop-and-go, driver override by brake. Only a few universities test ACC against standard test cases, so skip them.

figure.title: Adaptive cruise control loop
figure.aria: Set speed and measured radar gap form an error that the PI controller turns into throttle or brake action, with actual speed fed back.

chapters.example: The host car is set to 25 m/s and the radar sees a lead car doing 20 m/s at 60 m. The time gap is 60 m ÷ 25 m/s = 2.4 s. The target gap is 2.0 s, that is 2.0 × 25 = 50 m, so the gap error is +10 m and the controller reduces speed. The closing rate is 25 − 20 = 5 m/s, so at the present speeds the host would reach the lead car in 60 ÷ 5 = 12 s; the loop has 12 s to remove 5 m/s of speed, a comfortable deceleration of about 0.4 m/s².
chapters.trap: Basic cruise control cannot brake — only ACC has brake authority. Also, time gap is in seconds, not metres, and set speed is not the same as actual speed while the loop is still catching up.
chapters.prereq: Unit 4 for engine torque response to throttle; Unit 3 for radar and speed sensors.
chapters.leave: The full PI tuning method to 5.9; the radar signal processing chain to 5.8.

chapters.idea: Electric power steering uses a motor whose assist torque is mapped against steering torque and vehicle speed, replacing hydraulic pressure with a controlled current.
chapters.depth: Column, pinion and rack (dual pinion) EPS layouts; torque sensor built on a torsion bar with a Hall or inductive pick-up; steering angle sensor; motor and reduction gear; assist map, return-to-centre, damping and friction compensation; fail-safe back to manual steering; adaptive or variable-ratio steering that changes assist and ratio with speed. Some syllabi call the whole area 'adaptive power steering'. Hydraulic pumps and belt drives are background only.

figure.title: Electric power steering assist path
figure.aria: Driver torque and vehicle speed enter the EPS ECU, which sets motor current; a 10:1 reduction gear converts it into assist torque at the rack.

chapters.example: The assist map asks for 8 N·m at the pinion during parking and 2 N·m at 120 km/h. The reduction gear is 10:1 and the motor constant is 0.05 N·m per ampere. At parking: motor torque = 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8 N·m, so current = 0.8 ÷ 0.05 = 16 A. At 120 km/h: motor torque = 2 ÷ 10 = 0.2 N·m, current = 0.2 ÷ 0.05 = 4 A. The 4 A at highway speed keeps feel in the wheel instead of making it numb.
chapters.trap: More assist is not always better: assist must fall as speed rises. Students also confuse steering torque (driver input) with assist torque (motor output).
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for torque and angle sensors; unit 1 for the 12 V supply and motor current.
chapters.leave: Electric motor construction and drives; the vehicle network that carries speed to the ECU to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: ABS holds wheel slip near the peak of the friction curve by building, holding and releasing brake pressure many times a second, and traction control does the same with drive torque.
chapters.depth: Slip ratio λ = (v − ωr)/v; the μ–slip curve and its peak near λ = 0.1 to 0.2; wheel speed sensors (inductive or Hall); hydraulic modulator with inlet valve, outlet valve and return pump; the three pressure phases and a cycle rate of roughly 5 to 15 per second; EBD; traction control by throttle cut, ignition retard and braking the spinning wheel, plus the differential brake idea. Mention that ABS on loose gravel can lengthen a stop.

figure.aria: Two friction curves rise to a peak near 0.15 slip and then fall away, with the dry asphalt curve well above the wet road curve.

chapters.example: A car moves at v = 20 m/s, wheel radius r = 0.30 m, and the wheel turns at ω = 60 rad/s. Wheel speed at the contact patch = ωr = 60 × 0.30 = 18 m/s, so λ = (20 − 18)/20 = 0.10, inside the peak band and ABS leaves the pressure alone. If hard braking drops the wheel to ω = 40 rad/s, wheel speed = 12 m/s and λ = (20 − 12)/20 = 0.40, past the peak, so ABS releases pressure until slip returns near 0.15.
chapters.trap: Slip ratio uses the vehicle's forward speed as the reference, not the wheel speed, and it is dimensionless. Also, ABS does not always shorten a stop — on gravel or fresh snow it can lengthen it.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for wheel speed sensors; unit 1 for the hydraulic and electrical supply.
chapters.leave: Brake fluid, master cylinder and calliper design to a chassis course; the vehicle network to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: ESP compares the yaw rate the driver asked for with the yaw rate the car actually has, and brakes one wheel to create a correcting yaw moment.
chapters.depth: Sensors: yaw rate, lateral acceleration, steering angle, four wheel speeds and brake pressure; the bicycle-model reference yaw rate r = vδ/(L + K v²); understeer and oversteer, with the wheel that must be braked in each case; engine torque reduction; interaction with ABS and TCS; the ESP off switch and the limits set by tyre grip. Some syllabi call it ESC or VDC (vehicle dynamics control).

figure.title: ESP yaw-rate correction
figure.aria: Steering angle builds a desired yaw rate, compared with the measured yaw rate; the difference drives braking of one wheel to create a correcting yaw moment.

chapters.example: A car at v = 20 m/s is steered by δ = 0.05 rad (2.9°). Wheelbase L = 2.6 m and the understeer term K v² = 0.0025 × 400 = 1.0 m. Desired yaw rate r = vδ/(L + K v²) = (20 × 0.05)/(2.6 + 1.0) = 1.0/3.6 = 0.278 rad/s ≈ 15.9 °/s. The sensor reads 0.20 rad/s ≈ 11.5 °/s, so the car is understeering and the error is 0.078 rad/s. ESP brakes the rear inner wheel, which adds a yaw moment and turns the nose in.
chapters.trap: Braking the wrong wheel: understeer is corrected by braking the rear inner wheel and oversteer by braking the front outer wheel. ESP also cannot exceed tyre grip — it only helps the car do what the tyres allow.
chapters.prereq: 5.4 for slip, wheel speed and brake modulation; Unit 3 for the yaw rate and lateral acceleration sensors.
chapters.leave: Tyre modelling and vehicle dynamics beyond the bicycle model; sensor bus details to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: An active suspension drives a force actuator at each corner so the body stays flat while the wheels are left free to follow the road.
chapters.depth: Passive, semi-active (variable damper) and fully active (hydraulic or electric actuator); sensors: body accelerometer, wheel accelerometer, ride height; the skyhook damping law F = −c_sky × v_body; roll and pitch control by distributing forces across corners; bandwidth and power cost. Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it to the three layouts, one control law and one worked number.

figure.title: Skyhook damper loop
figure.aria: Road input acts on the suspension, the corner body velocity feeds the skyhook controller, and damper current closes the loop back into the suspension.

chapters.example: The skyhook gain is c_sky = 5000 N·s/m and the body moves upward at v_body = 0.08 m/s. Required force F = c_sky × v_body = 5000 × 0.08 = 400 N. The damper delivers 800 N per ampere of current, so the controller commands 400 ÷ 800 = 0.5 A. A larger body velocity, say 0.16 m/s, would ask for 800 N and 1.0 A, which is the limit of this damper.
chapters.trap: Skyhook damps the body, not the wheel, and the sign of the body velocity decides whether the actuator pulls or pushes. Reversing the sign gives a suspension that adds to body motion instead of removing it.
chapters.prereq: Basic spring–mass–damper vibration from a mechanics course; 5.5 for yaw and roll control using brakes.
chapters.leave: Hydraulic actuator design and ride comfort rating methods; only the control idea is examinable here.

chapters.idea: Passive safety absorbs crash energy and restrains the occupants, and an airbag is a supplement to the seat belt fired by a crash sensor within milliseconds.
chapters.depth: Crumple zones and the crash pulse; seat belt, pretensioner and load limiter; airbag ECU with accelerometer and safing sensor; squib and gas generator; bag venting; side, curtain and knee airbags; rollover sensing; occupant detection and child seat rules; deployment threshold and why an unbelted occupant can be injured by the bag. Keep the chemistry of the gas generator to one line.

figure.aria: A timeline in milliseconds: the crash pulse lasts 86 ms, the ECU detects in 10 ms and fires at 20 ms, the bag fills by 50 ms and the occupant rides it down afterwards.

chapters.example: A car at 50 km/h (13.9 m/s) stops in a crumple zone of s = 0.6 m. Average deceleration a = v²/(2s) = 13.9² ÷ (2 × 0.6) = 193 ÷ 1.2 = 161 m/s² ≈ 16.4 g. Time to stop = v/a = 13.9 ÷ 161 = 0.086 s, that is 86 ms. The bag must be full and venting well before the occupant arrives, which is why detection at 10 to 15 ms and full inflation near 50 ms matter.
chapters.trap: An airbag does not replace the seat belt, and it is not fired by a small bump — the ECU needs deceleration above a threshold held for a set time, plus agreement from the safing sensor.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for accelerometers; unit 1 for the electrical supply and squib circuit.
chapters.leave: Detailed occupant kinematics and crash-test standards; belt geometry design.

chapters.idea: ADAS is a stack of sensors, perception, fusion, planning and actuation that warns the driver or acts for a moment, at a defined level of automation.
chapters.depth: SAE levels 0 to 5; camera, radar, lidar and ultrasonic sensors and their trade-offs in range, cost and weather; functions: AEB, lane departure warning and lane keep, blind spot detection, adaptive cruise as an ADAS function, traffic sign recognition, parking assist, driver monitoring; sensor fusion; the link to functional safety. Only a few universities teach ADAS as a full chapter, so keep the focus on the layers and one or two functions.

figure.aria: Five layers from raw sensors at the bottom through perception, fusion and planning up to actuation at the top.

chapters.example: An AEB system at 50 km/h (13.9 m/s) has 0.5 s of sensing and brake-build delay before 8 m/s² of braking starts. Distance in the delay = 13.9 × 0.5 = 6.9 m. Braking distance = v²/(2a) = 193 ÷ 16 = 12.1 m. Total = 19.0 m. If the radar detects the stopped car at 25 m, the margin is 25 − 19.0 = 6.0 m, so the stop is possible. At 30 m of detection the margin is 11 m; at 18 m the system cannot avoid the crash and can only reduce the impact speed.
chapters.trap: Level 2 is not self-driving — the driver still monitors the road — and a warning function (lane departure warning) is not the same as an intervening function (lane keep).
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for adaptive cruise; 5.3 for steering angle; 5.7 for passive safety as the last resort.
chapters.leave: Formal ISO 26262 safety analysis and V2X communication to Unit 6; deep-learning perception details.

chapters.idea: A PI controller removes the steady-state speed error, a PD controller adds damping, and two gains plus a plant model are all a speed loop needs.
chapters.depth: Plant as a first-order lag from force to speed, m dv/dt = F − b v, giving gain K and time constant τ; error e = v_ref − v; PI law u = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt; PD law u = Kp e + Kd de/dt; gain selection by lambda tuning, Kp = τ/(K λ), Ti = τ, Ki = Kp/Ti; the offset left by proportional action alone; derivative on the measurement to avoid noise; PI with a reference model, where a model of the plant pre-shapes the setpoint before the loop sees it. Only a few universities teach this, so keep to one plant and one tuning.

figure.title: PI speed loop for a 1500 kg vehicle
figure.aria: A reference speed of 30 m/s minus the measured speed forms the error; the PI block turns it into tractive force, the vehicle responds, and the measured speed closes the loop.

chapters.example: Vehicle mass m = 1500 kg, resistance b = 100 N per m/s, so 1500 dv/dt = F − 100v and V(s)/F(s) = 1/(1500s + 100) = 0.01/(15s + 1). Plant gain K = 0.01 (m/s) per N, time constant τ = 15 s. Choose a closed-loop time constant λ = 3 s: Kp = τ/(K λ) = 15 ÷ (0.01 × 3) = 500 N per (m/s). Take Ti = τ = 15 s, so Ki = Kp/Ti = 500 ÷ 15 = 33.3 N per (m/s·s). Check the purpose of Ki: to hold 30 m/s against 100 × 30 = 3000 N of resistance, proportional action alone would need an error of 3000 ÷ 500 = 6 m/s; the integral term supplies the 3000 N and the error falls to zero.
chapters.trap: Getting the error sign wrong (it is reference minus measured) and forgetting that Kp alone leaves a steady offset — the integral term removes it. A derivative term on a noisy measured speed amplifies noise unless it is filtered.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for the cruise control loop this replaces; basic Laplace transforms and first-order lag from a control course.
chapters.leave: Full frequency-domain design, Bode and root locus, to a control systems course; digital sampling and PWM details to Unit 6.
